selection_reason: 1. Evidence: no experiments have been run yet, so we have no data on any design factor (modality, single vs. multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation, fusion). 2. What this tests: config_036 is a central anchor. It is multimodal and multiprofile, which I expect to be competitive, and uses a mid-sized RNA encoder (scVI with 200 dimensions) and a strong image encoder (ImageNet ViT-L). It also uses the simplest aggregation (average pooling) and the simplest fusion (concatenation). This gives a reasonably strong first result without committing to the more complex transformer aggregation or weighted fusion. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: later experiments can change one factor at a time from this anchor. That includes switching to RNA-only or image-only, to single-profile, to transformer aggregation, to weighted fusion, or to a different encoder. Each of these comparisons then isolates the effect of one design choice, which is more informative under a limited budget than starting from a minimal baseline far from the likely optimum.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: There is only one result so far. config_036 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) reached 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. We do not yet know how much of this comes from the image branch versus the RNA branch. 2) What this tests: config_005 keeps everything the same except that it removes the image modality (RNA-only, scVI, multiprofile, avgpool). This one-factor change shows directly whether adding images improves on RNA alone. 3) Why now: Whether to use multimodal input is the decision with the widest consequences in this search space. Answering it first tells us whether to spend the remaining budget on fusion, image-encoder and aggregation variants, or on RNA-encoder choices. That makes it a better use of one experiment than fine-tuning secondary settings such as aggregation or fusion type.

Evidence: with the scvi_n200 RNA encoder and avgpool aggregation fixed, multimodal concat with imagenet_vit_l scored 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. RNA-only scored 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1, about 6.5 points lower. Uncertainty: we cannot yet tell whether this gain comes from combining the two modalities or simply from the image features alone. Test: image-only imagenet_vit_l with avgpool uses the same image encoder, profile setting and aggregation, so it completes the RNA-only, image-only and multimodal comparison. If image-only is close to 0.715, RNA adds little, and future runs should focus on image encoders and aggregation rather than RNA encoders or fusion. If it is clearly lower, the two modalities are complementary, and tuning fusion, aggregation and RNA encoder within multimodal configurations is justified. Why now: this question decides which design dimensions deserve the remaining budget, so it is a better use of one experiment than a single-dimension tweak of the current best.

1) Evidence: the multimodal model (config_036, scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) scored best at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. RNA-only reached 0.650 and image-only only 0.332, so the RNA signal carries most of the performance and the image adds a meaningful amount on top. Every run so far used avgpool, so we do not know whether aggregation matters. That is a major untested design axis for multiprofile inputs. 2) Test: config_038 changes only avgpool to transformer and keeps the rest of the best configuration fixed. This isolates whether learned, attention-based aggregation across profiles beats simple mean pooling. 3) Why now: it is a one-factor exploitation of the current best direction, so the result is directly interpretable as an aggregation effect. If the transformer helps, it becomes the new base for later tests of the RNA encoder (scGPT, PCA) and the fusion method (weighted). If it does not, we can confidently use the cheaper avgpool for the rest of the budget.

1. Evidence: multimodal models (about 0.715 to 0.721 accuracy) clearly beat RNA-only (0.650) and image-only (0.332). RNA is therefore the dominant signal and images add a useful complement. Aggregation looks like a minor factor: transformer beat avgpool by about 0.006 in accuracy, but avgpool had slightly higher F1, so the result is inconclusive. The RNA encoder has never been varied (only scvi_n200 tested), and RNA carries most of the predictive signal, so this is the largest untested source of uncertainty. 2. This experiment keeps the best multimodal setup (multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) and swaps scvi_n200 for scGPT. Any change can then be attributed to the RNA encoder alone. 3. Under a limited budget, this tests the design choice most likely to move performance substantially and stays within the promising multimodal region. Fusion type and image encoder are worth testing later, but they likely have smaller effects given that the image modality is weak.

1. Evidence: multimodal scVI plus ViT-L is the clear best direction, at about 0.715–0.721 accuracy. It beats RNA-only (0.650) by a wide margin, while image-only is weak (0.332). Avgpool and transformer aggregation are nearly tied: transformer is slightly higher on accuracy, avgpool slightly higher on F1, so aggregation looks minor. scGPT clearly underperforms scVI. Fusion strategy has never been tested; every multimodal run so far used concat. 2. This experiment keeps the best-performing setup (scVI, ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer) and swaps concat for weighted fusion. That isolates the effect of fusion directly. Weighted fusion is a plausible improvement here because the image modality is much weaker than RNA, and learned modality weighting could down-weight noisy image features. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: it builds on the strongest region of the search space and resolves an entirely unexplored design axis with a single controlled comparison. The result will tell us whether fusion should be fixed or explored further before spending runs on secondary axes such as the image encoder or PCA features.

1) Evidence: RNA is the dominant modality. RNA-only scvi reached 0.650, while image-only ViT-L reached only 0.332. The RNA encoder choice has the largest observed effect: swapping scvi for scGPT dropped accuracy from about 0.72 to 0.51. Aggregation and fusion changes within scvi+ViT-L produced only small gains (0.715 to 0.725), and F1 moved inconsistently, so those are fine-tuning details rather than major levers. pca_n2000 is the one RNA encoder never tested. 2) This experiment swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000 in the current best setup (ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion). Comparing it directly with config_039 shows whether scvi is truly the best RNA representation or whether a simpler, higher-dimensional PCA input works as well or better. 3) Because the RNA encoder has the largest demonstrated impact and pca_n2000 is a complete unknown, this test reduces the most important remaining uncertainty. It also has a realistic chance of beating the current best. Testing resnet50 or singleprofile can come next, since the image branch contributes less.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The broad choices look settled. scVI beats scGPT and PCA, multiprofile beats singleprofile, and multimodal beats RNA-only and image-only. Within the top region (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile), the remaining choices show only small, single-run gaps. avgpool+concat scored 0.715, transformer+concat 0.721 and transformer+weighted 0.725, with F1 roughly flat at 0.681-0.687. This separates the effect of aggregation from the effect of fusion and shows whether they interact. If avgpool+weighted roughly matches transformer+weighted, the costlier transformer aggregation is not clearly justified, and fusion becomes the more important lever. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: It is a low-risk, high-information follow-up in the most promising region, so it can also produce a top result. Settling these two design questions before spending budget on other comparisons, such as ResNet50 vs ViT-L, avoids misreading small differences.
